p: Jeskyns is still a youngster as woods go. It opened in the 2000s, when Forestry England's predecessor turned former arable fields into a public woodland, and you can see the landscape changing year by year as the trees grow up. That openness is part of its charm: big skies, wildflowers in summer and plenty of room to fly a kite or kick a ball. Horse riders are welcome on the bridleways too, so keep an eye out and give them space.

In late summer and autumn, the orchards are a highlight, with old varieties of fruit trees that nod to Kent's reputation as the Garden of England. It's a lovely season for a family wander, especially when the leaves start to turn and the paths are crunchy underfoot.
Allow a couple of hours, or longer with a picnic and a kite. If you've got the energy for more walking, Shorne Woods Country Park is close by, with its own trails, play areas and lakes.

Cobham village is right on the doorstep and has strong links to Charles Dickens, who loved walking here. The Leather Bottle pub features in The Pickwick Papers. In Gravesend, find the statue of Pocahontas at St George's Church, where she was buried in 1617, then stroll down to the river to watch the ships on the Thames. Rochester, with its castle, cathedral and Dickensian high street, is a short drive along the A2 too.
